paragraphs: This paper investigates how easily a language model’s safety behavior can be disrupted by changing a small part of the model. The researchers use pruning and low-rank modifications to locate regions important for safety guardrails. They examine whether these regions can be separated from regions that support the model’s usefulness.

The identified regions are sparse: about 3% at the parameter level and 2.5% at the rank level. Removing them weakens safety without significantly reducing utility in the reported study. This separation matters because a model can retain much of its useful behavior while losing protections; preserved utility alone therefore does not establish that safety alignment has survived a modification.

The study also tests whether restricting changes to these safety-critical regions prevents attacks through fine-tuning. The models remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even with those restrictions. Together, these findings support the authors’ conclusion that safety alignment is brittle and that protecting the identified regions alone is insufficient in the settings examined.
icml-2024-assessing-the-brittleness-of-s.tldr: Small, identifiable model regions can be critical for safety, yet protecting them still leaves models vulnerable to fine-tuning attacks.

paragraphs: Universal domain adaptation handles two changes at once: examples look different across domains, and the domains do not necessarily contain the same categories. A successful model must recognize unfamiliar target categories while avoiding assignments to categories that occur only in the source domain. BSP-WSA addresses both problems within one approach.

An adversarial classifier identifies unknown target categories and helps align feature distributions across domains. The method then applies singular value decomposition to the classifier’s outputs, increasing larger singular values and decreasing smaller ones. The authors propose this polarization as a way to reduce mistaken assignments of target examples to source-only categories.

A second component generates additional data for categories shared by the domains through weighted semantic augmentation. This focuses augmentation on the categories where cross-domain transfer is relevant. Experiments on three benchmarks show that BSP-WSA can outperform existing leading universal adaptation methods. The findings support combining unknown-category handling, structured classifier outputs, and shared-category augmentation when both category membership and feature distributions change.
icml-2024-batch-singular-value-polarizat.tldr: BSP-WSA combines classifier-output polarization and shared-category augmentation to improve adaptation when domains differ in both appearance and categories.

paragraphs: Boximator gives users a spatial way to control movement in generated videos. Users first select objects in a conditioning frame with hard boxes. They then specify boxes in future frames to describe an object’s position, shape, or motion path. Hard and soft boxes allow these instructions to be more exact or more approximate.

The system attaches to existing video diffusion models as a control module. During training, the original model weights remain frozen, preserving the base model’s learned knowledge while the new module learns motion control. A self-tracking technique simplifies learning the relationship between boxes and the objects they are supposed to constrain.

The experiments report state-of-the-art FVD video-quality scores, improvements over two base models, and further gains when box constraints are supplied. Large improvements in bounding-box alignment support the claimed motion control, while human evaluators prefer Boximator’s videos over the base model’s outputs. These results connect the control interface to both measured instruction alignment and perceived output quality.
icml-2024-boximator-generating-rich-and-.tldr: Boximator adds box-based motion control to video diffusion models while improving reported video quality and user preference.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participants use different kinds of models. FedType addresses this model heterogeneity by giving each client a small proxy model with the same design. These proxies provide a common mechanism for exchanging information while clients retain their larger private models.

The central challenge is transferring knowledge between each private model and its smaller proxy. FedType uses uncertainty-based asymmetrical reciprocity learning for this exchange, allowing the two models to contribute through an asymmetric learning relationship. The approach does not require public data, so its knowledge-transfer mechanism avoids depending on a shared public dataset.

The small, identical proxies serve several purposes together: bridging differences between private models, supporting model security, and lowering communication costs. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness and generalization across diverse settings. The contribution is a framework in which clients can collaborate despite model differences, with knowledge exchange handled through lightweight intermediaries. Its reported benefits concern that combination of heterogeneous participation, private models, and efficient communication.
icml-2024-bridging-model-heterogeneity-i.tldr: FedType uses small shared-design proxy models to connect heterogeneous private models without requiring public data.

paragraphs: Cross-domain offline reinforcement learning tries to reduce the target domain’s data needs by reusing previously collected source data. The difficulty is that the same actions can produce different transitions in different domains. Simply combining the datasets can therefore hurt performance, making the choice of which source transitions to share important.

The paper learns representations through a contrastive objective built from transitions sampled across domains. The authors show that this objective recovers a mutual-information gap between the domains’ transition functions. Their formulation avoids an unbounded-gap issue that arises when handling substantially different domains. The learned contrastive scores then guide a filtering algorithm that selectively transfers source transitions.

Experiments across several tasks support the value of selecting data through these representations. With only 10% of the target data, the method reaches 89.2% of the performance obtained by state-of-the-art methods using the full target dataset. This result indicates that carefully filtered source experience can substantially reduce target-data requirements in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-contrastive-representation-for.tldr: Contrastively learned transition representations help filter source data, reducing target-data needs in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A classifier deployed in a new setting may face both unfamiliar-looking examples and entirely new categories. This paper studies those challenges together: assigning examples to previously seen classes while discovering unseen classes under a domain shift. Handling only novel categories or only changes in feature distributions leaves part of this problem unresolved.

The proposed method, CROW, uses prototypes and a cluster-then-match strategy. It starts from the structured representation space supplied by foundation models, groups examples into clusters, and matches those clusters with previously seen classes. This matching process supports discovery of novel classes while preserving a connection to categories already known to the model.

CROW then fine-tunes the representation space with an objective designed for this combined discovery setting. Across image-classification benchmarks, the authors report an average performance improvement of 8% over alternative baselines across 75 experimental settings. The results support treating recognition and discovery as linked tasks when domain changes make the relationship between examples and known classes harder to establish.
icml-2024-cross-domain-open-world-discov.tldr: CROW clusters and matches foundation-model representations to recognize known classes and discover new ones under domain shift.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups samples using several views of the same underlying data. These views can provide information that is shared across them or complementary between them. When some samples lack particular views, the clustering method has less information available for identifying those relationships and forming useful groups.

The paper proposes a diffusion-based missing-view generation network, called DMVG, to recover the absent views. This makes reconstruction of missing information an explicit part of incomplete multi-view learning. The approach goes beyond concentrating only on the views already present, allowing generated views to contribute to the subsequent clustering process.

For situations with high rates of missing data, the authors also introduce an incomplete multi-view data augmentation strategy intended to improve reconstruction quality. Experiments report both accurate missing-view prediction and better downstream clustering than several leading incomplete multi-view clustering methods. These are distinct benefits: the generated information resembles the missing views, and its use improves the task for which those views are needed.
icml-2024-diffusion-based-missing-view-g.tldr: DMVG generates missing data views with diffusion and improves subsequent clustering in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The diffusion protein language model, DPLM, is designed to both generate protein sequences and learn representations useful for prediction. It is pretrained on evolutionary-scale sequence data using a self-supervised discrete diffusion framework. The same generative training foundation supports several downstream uses, rather than restricting the model to a single protein task.

After pretraining, DPLM generates novel, diverse sequences with plausible structures without requiring a conditioning input. Its learned representations can also be fine-tuned for predictive tasks, where the paper reports favorable comparisons with ESM2. These findings connect generative pretraining with both sequence creation and useful representations of protein information.

The authors additionally demonstrate several forms of controlled generation. DPLM can build scaffolds around partial peptide sequences, including functional motifs, with a reported high success rate. It can use structural information for inverse folding or classifier guidance to steer sequences toward desired properties such as specified secondary structures. Together, these applications demonstrate flexibility in what information can guide sequence generation.
icml-2024-diffusion-language-models-are-.tldr: DPLM uses diffusion pretraining to support protein generation, predictive representation learning, and several forms of controlled sequence design.

paragraphs: Soft analytical side-channel attacks combine physical leakage with knowledge of a cryptographic algorithm. Leakage supplies uncertain predictions about intermediate computations, and the algorithm’s logic helps combine them into probabilities over the secret key. A common inference method, loopy belief propagation, lacks guarantees about convergence and the quality of its resulting inference.

ExSASCA replaces that inference procedure with knowledge compilation and tractable probabilistic circuits. The goal is to compute the relevant probabilities exactly while keeping the computation practical. Exactness here concerns the inference over the probabilistic information supplied to the attack; the physical leakage still provides uncertain evidence about intermediate values.

In the reported AES evaluation, ExSASCA improves top-1 success rate by more than 31 percentage points over SASCA. With sparse belief messages, its computational cost is only slightly higher than SASCA’s and roughly three orders of magnitude below exhaustive exact inference. Even with dense messages, it uses six times fewer computations than exhaustive inference. The results show substantial gains in attack success without requiring exhaustive enumeration.
icml-2024-exact-soft-analytical-side-cha.tldr: ExSASCA makes side-channel inference exact with probabilistic circuits, improving reported AES attack success at far less cost than exhaustive inference.

paragraphs: Learning to defer lets a model hand decisions to a human expert. Training such a system requires a rule for deciding when the model should answer and when the expert should take over. The paper argues that the usual formulation of Bayes optimality overlooks dependence between the model and the expert.

The authors introduce dependent Bayes optimality, a formulation that makes this relationship part of the deferral decision. This matters because the usefulness of handing off a decision depends on the model and expert together. Their dependence can contain information relevant to choosing who should decide, beyond what the original formulation captures.

From this formulation, the researchers derive a deferral principle and use it to construct a consistent surrogate loss. Consistency connects the training objective to the desired optimal decision rule. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show advantages for the proposed method. The contribution thus links a revised theoretical target to a trainable objective and empirical improvements in human–AI decision allocation.
icml-2024-exploiting-human-ai-dependence.tldr: Accounting for dependence between a model and a human expert yields a new optimality formulation and improved learning-to-defer objective.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a neural network’s complexity while trying to preserve its performance. This paper investigates whether intrinsic dimension can help decide what to prune in vision-language models. Intrinsic dimension describes how many dimensions are needed to represent data that occupies a lower-dimensional structure within a larger space.

The researchers examine variation in intrinsic dimension across large pretrained vision-language models and study how the visual and language modalities contribute to prunability. They propose a layer-importance measure based on intrinsic dimension that can be combined with existing pruning metrics. The motivation is to connect the complexity of learned representations with decisions about which parts of a model can be reduced.

Experiments find a strong correlation between intrinsic dimension and modality prunability. Visual representations are more sensitive and more crucial to performance, while language representations are more robust to pruning. These empirical results support an asymmetric pruning strategy guided by intrinsic dimension, rather than assuming that visual and language components should undergo the same degree of reduction.
icml-2024-exploring-intrinsic-dimension-.tldr: Intrinsic dimension helps guide vision-language model pruning, with experiments supporting greater pruning of language representations than visual ones.

paragraphs: Test-time augmentation combines predictions from transformed versions of an input. Standard forms rely on transformations that preserve the label, which restricts the transformations available for combinatorial problems. MAgg expands this approach by using metamorphic relations: relationships between transformed instances that can remain useful even when their labels need not be identical.

The method represents these relations as directed graphs and supplies the graphs to a graph neural network. That network improves how predictions across transformed instances are aggregated. The key idea is that the relationship between instances provides structure for combining their predictions, allowing the aggregation process to use more than label-preserving transformations.

The researchers evaluate MAgg on Boolean satisfiability prediction, decision traveling-salesman satisfiability prediction, and graph edit distance estimation. They report significant improvements over the base models in all three tasks. The findings support the method’s versatility across the tested combinatorial problems and show that inference-time augmentation can benefit from explicitly modeling relations among transformed inputs.
icml-2024-extending-test-time-augmentati.tldr: MAgg uses graph-modeled relations between transformed inputs to extend test-time augmentation beyond label-preserving transformations.

paragraphs: Directed evolution searches for protein mutations that improve functionality. KnowRLM brings biochemical knowledge into this search alongside patterns learned from protein sequences. The authors motivate this combination by observing that existing machine-learning-assisted methods often emphasize data-driven strategies while overlooking available knowledge about amino acids.

The method constructs an amino acid knowledge graph to represent biochemical relationships. A protein-language-model policy then samples mutants through preferential random walks on this graph, using a dynamic sliding window. This lets contextual sequence information and biochemical relationships both influence which candidate mutations the system explores.

An active learning loop connects candidate generation with fitness prediction. Newly proposed mutants are actively sampled to fine-tune a fitness predictor, which supplies rewards back to the knowledge-aware policy. The system consequently updates its search using feedback rather than relying on a fixed predictor throughout. Experiments report more efficient identification of high-fitness mutants than existing methods, supporting the value of combining sequence statistics, domain knowledge, and iterative feedback.
icml-2024-knowledge-aware-reinforced-lan.tldr: KnowRLM combines protein language models, amino acid knowledge graphs, and active learning to identify high-fitness mutants more efficiently.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition deals with training data in which some classes occur much more frequently than others. Many approaches target evaluation data with equal class frequencies, but deployment may involve an unknown and uneven class distribution. This paper studies how to correct predictions when that test distribution is not known in advance.

The theoretical motivation is conditional: precisely estimating test-time class frequencies can substantially reduce generalization error. The proposed label shift correction method, LSC, estimates those frequencies through a generalized black box shift estimation framework. It then adjusts a pretrained model’s predictions to better match the estimated test distribution.

Experiments report significant improvements over previous leading approaches, especially for nonuniform test distributions. LSC also complements existing long-tail learning methods and consistently improves their performance in the reported evaluations. Its contribution is therefore a correction mechanism that can be applied alongside existing approaches. The theory identifies accurate distribution estimation as a key condition behind the potential reduction in generalization error.
icml-2024-learning-label-shift-correctio.tldr: LSC estimates unknown test-time class frequencies and adjusts pretrained predictions to improve long-tailed recognition.

paragraphs: Deep denoisers can help reconstruct signals and images in inverse problems, but convergence guarantees often require constraints on their behavior. Conditions such as non-expansiveness can reduce recovery quality when enforced during training. This paper investigates pseudo-contractiveness as a weaker constraint that can support convergence while giving the denoiser more flexibility.

The authors analyze the spectrum of the denoiser’s Jacobian to relate different assumptions about its behavior. They derive algorithms using gradient descent and the Ishikawa process. With the stronger assumption of strict pseudo-contractiveness, they also obtain efficient methods based on half-quadratic splitting and forward-backward splitting.

The proposed algorithms have theoretical guarantees of strong convergence to a fixed point under their associated assumptions. A training strategy based on holomorphic transformations and functional calculi enforces the pseudo-contractive property. Experiments show superior performance relative to related denoisers and competitive visual and quantitative reconstruction results. The contribution connects a less restrictive training condition with both mathematical convergence analysis and empirical recovery quality.
icml-2024-learning-pseudo-contractive-de.tldr: Training pseudo-contractive denoisers relaxes common constraints while supporting convergent reconstruction algorithms and strong empirical recovery performance.

paragraphs: A neural surrogate is a network trained to imitate a program’s behavior. Such models can support input tuning, adaptation, and faster computation. Traditionally, each surrogate learns from input-output examples for one program. Another approach asks a language model to consume program text and act as the surrogate itself, creating an accuracy–resource tradeoff.

Neural surrogate compilation separates the creation of the surrogate from its execution. The compiler reads program text and produces a neural network that serves as the surrogate. The authors implement this idea with hypernetworks trained on a dataset of C programs, using learned program-to-network generation instead of coupling both roles inside one language model.

Compared with training surrogates from scratch, the generated surrogates are reported to be 1.91–9.50 times as data-efficient and to train in 4.31–7.28 times fewer epochs. These findings support learning a reusable compilation mechanism across programs. The reported gains concern the data and training epochs needed for the resulting surrogates, rather than establishing a universal execution-speed improvement.
icml-2024-learning-to-compile-programs-t.tldr: Hypernetworks compile C program text into neural surrogates that require less training data and fewer epochs than training from scratch.

paragraphs: Magicoder is a family of code language models with no more than seven billion parameters, released with code, weights, and training data. Its central contribution is OSS-Instruct, a method that uses open-source code snippets to inspire synthetic coding instructions. The motivation is to make generated training data more diverse, realistic, and controllable.

The models train on 75,000 synthetic instruction examples. Grounding instruction generation in existing code is intended to reduce biases inherent in language-model-generated data. OSS-Instruct can also be combined with other data-generation approaches, including Evol-Instruct; the authors use that compatibility to produce the enhanced MagicoderS models.

Across coding benchmarks, Magicoder and MagicoderS substantially outperform leading models of similar or larger sizes. One reported comparison has CodeLlama-based MagicoderS-CL-7B scoring 66.5 versus ChatGPT’s 65.9 in pass@1 on HumanEval+. That specific result illustrates the reported benchmark strength without implying superiority on every coding task. The broader contribution is evidence that open-source code can provide useful grounding for synthetic instruction creation.
icml-2024-magicoder-empowering-code-gene.tldr: Magicoder uses open-source code to ground synthetic instructions, producing small code models with strong reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Models that learn latent representations can produce different embeddings when methods, datasets, or hyperparameters change. PRESTO treats this collection of possible representations as an object of study. Its goal is to make variability across these choices measurable, helping researchers understand sensitivity rather than examining each embedding in isolation.

The framework uses persistent homology to characterize latent spaces. Those characterizations support pairwise similarity and dissimilarity measurements as well as statistical reasoning about distributions of representations. This creates a common basis for comparing embeddings produced by diverse combinations of modeling and data choices.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that the pipeline preserves desirable properties of collections of latent representations. They also demonstrate uses in sensitivity analysis, anomalous-embedding detection, and efficient hyperparameter search. These applications matter because differences between embeddings can reveal unstable choices or unusual outcomes, while similarities can help organize a search. PRESTO offers a framework for analyzing that wider landscape of learned representations.
icml-2024-mapping-the-multiverse-of-late.tldr: PRESTO uses persistent homology to compare latent representations and support sensitivity analysis, anomaly detection, and hyperparameter search.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can use separate learning objectives for individual modalities to reduce imbalanced learning. This paper identifies a complication: gradients from those unimodal objectives can conflict with gradients from the combined multimodal objective. Such conflicts can push the individual encoders in directions that undermine their optimization.

The authors observe that the easier multimodal loss has smaller gradient magnitude and covariance than the unimodal loss. They use this discrepancy to analyze Pareto integration in the multimodal setting and design MMPareto. The algorithm seeks a final gradient direction shared by all objectives, with increased magnitude intended to improve generalization.

Experiments across multiple modalities and frameworks with dense cross-modal interactions report superior performance and support the method’s extensibility. The findings suggest that individual-modality assistance benefits from explicitly managing its interaction with the combined objective. The authors also anticipate applicability to multitask settings with clear differences in task difficulty; that broader use is presented as an expectation rather than an established result across all multitask problems.
icml-2024-mmpareto-boosting-multimodal-l.tldr: MMPareto reconciles conflicting unimodal and multimodal training gradients to improve learning across the evaluated modalities and frameworks.

paragraphs: This paper examines why strong representations learned from public data can improve downstream learning with differential privacy. The authors analyze a layer-peeled representation model that exhibits neural collapse. This provides a setting for studying how the quality and geometry of learned features interact with private learning.

Within that setting, they show that misclassification error becomes independent of dimension when actual features are sufficiently close to ideal features. The distance threshold is an essential condition of the result. Empirical analysis of last-layer features also finds that more powerful pretrained models produce better representations, connecting the theoretical focus on feature quality to observed model behavior.

The study additionally finds that private fine-tuning is less robust than nonprivate fine-tuning, particularly under perturbations. Theory and experiments motivate feature normalization and dimension reduction as ways to improve robustness. Applying PCA to last-layer features significantly improves test accuracy in the reported experiments. The findings highlight both representation quality and feature processing as relevant to effective private fine-tuning.
icml-2024-neural-collapse-meets-differen.tldr: Neural-collapse analysis links high-quality features to private learning, while experiments show that PCA can improve private fine-tuning accuracy.

paragraphs: As AI and machine-learning conferences publish thousands of papers, researchers face a growing challenge in deciding what to read. This position paper studies social media influencers as part of that discovery process. It examines whether the papers they highlight receive more citations and considers the responsibilities that accompany this visibility.

The analysis uses a dataset of more than 8,000 papers and controls matched on nine key covariates. Statistical and causal inference analyses find significantly higher citations for influencer-endorsed papers, whose median citation counts are two to three times those of the control group. This is a finding about the studied groups, rather than a promise that endorsement will produce the same increase for any particular paper.

The researchers also investigate the geographic, gender, and institutional diversity of highlighted authors. Their position is that influencers have a place in academic communication and should curate responsibly. They advocate journalistic standards that include a diverse selection of topics, authors, and institutions, linking the observed visibility advantage to responsibilities in choosing what research receives attention.
icml-2024-position-ai-ml-influencers-hav.tldr: Influencer-endorsed papers had higher citations in a matched study, motivating a call for responsible and diverse research curation.

paragraphs: Admission control decides which arriving jobs enter a queue when jobs offer different rewards and incur holding costs. This paper studies learning that policy for an M/M/c/S queue with multiple job classes. The challenge is to obtain useful regret guarantees by exploiting the queue’s structure instead of relying only on bounds for general reinforcement-learning problems.

General regret bounds involve the diameter of the underlying Markov decision process, and queueing systems can have diameters exponential in buffer size. That makes diameter-dependent guarantees prohibitive for practical use. The authors develop an algorithm inspired by UCRL2 and analyze it using structural properties of the admission-control problem.

For finitely many servers, the expected total regret is bounded by O(S log T + sqrt(mT log T)), where S is buffer size, m is the number of job classes, and T is elapsed time. With infinitely many servers, the authors prove that dependence on S disappears. These results establish sharper guarantees for this structured setting without contradicting worst-case bounds for general problems.
icml-2024-reinforcement-learning-and-reg.tldr: An admission-control learning algorithm exploits queue structure to obtain regret bounds that avoid exponential dependence on buffer size.

paragraphs: Multiple-choice questions make language models easy to score, but choosing an answer may not reflect how well a model responds to an open-ended request. This paper evaluates 24 models across 11 benchmarks and identifies potential drawbacks in multiple-choice assessment, including inconsistencies with models’ behavior when generating open-ended answers.

The authors introduce RWQ-Elo, which compares models in a two-player competitive format and assigns Elo ratings. GPT-4 judges the comparisons. To make the questions closer to practical use, the researchers compile a Real-world Questions benchmark containing 20,772 authentic user inquiries. The evaluation therefore centers on generated responses to user questions.

The study analyzes the rating system and compares it with earlier leaderboards, including Alpaca Eval and MT-Bench. The authors report stability and the feasibility of adding new models. These findings support RWQ-Elo as a potential alternative for assessing generative performance. Its ratings specifically reflect the proposed question collection, pairwise comparison process, and GPT-4 judging arrangement.
icml-2024-rethinking-generative-large-la.tldr: RWQ-Elo evaluates open-ended answers to authentic user questions through GPT-4-judged pairwise comparisons and Elo ratings.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can struggle when deployed in a situation that differs from its training environment, even if the new situation has similar meaning. SiT addresses this generalization problem through the visual representations used by the policy. It is a scalable vision transformer that learns from both local and global patterns through self-supervision.

Its central component is Graph Symmetric Attention, a modification of ordinary self-attention designed to preserve graph symmetries. This produces invariant and equivariant latent representations: representations that remain unchanged or change in a corresponding way under the relevant symmetries. The architecture therefore incorporates structure into how visual information is represented.

The authors report better generalization than vision transformers on MiniGrid and Procgen reinforcement-learning benchmarks. They also demonstrate sample efficiency on Atari 100k and CIFAR10. Together, these results support symmetry-aware attention as a useful design choice for learning transferable representations. The evidence spans generalization and sample efficiency in the named evaluations, connecting the architectural change to practical learning behavior.
icml-2024-sit-symmetry-invariant-transfo.tldr: SiT incorporates graph symmetries into transformer attention to improve reported generalization and sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Data-free meta-learning extracts knowledge from pretrained models without accessing their original training data, aiming to adapt quickly to unseen tasks. This paper studies what happens when those models are heterogeneous. Differences between their tasks can create conflicting learning signals and reduce the quality of the resulting meta-model.

The authors identify a tradeoff: more homogeneous models reduce task conflicts but increase overfitting risk. Task Groupings Regularization addresses this by embedding pretrained models in a task space, measuring their dissimilarity, and grouping heterogeneous models together. Within each group, implicit gradient regularization reduces conflicts while encouraging a learning direction suitable for all tasks.

This strategy seeks to preserve the benefits of diverse tasks while making their contributions compatible enough to learn shared representations. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report superior performance, including challenging settings involving different domains and model architectures. The findings support treating heterogeneity as something to organize and manage, with grouping and gradient regularization working together to improve cross-task generalization.
icml-2024-task-groupings-regularization-.tldr: Task Groupings Regularization organizes heterogeneous pretrained models and reduces task-gradient conflicts for data-free meta-learning.
